title: Nitroglycerin
wiki_lead:
Nitroglycerin (NG, alternative spelling nitroglycerine), also known as trinitroglycerin (TNG), nitro, glyceryl trinitrate (GTN), or 1,2,3-trinitroxypropane, is a dense, colorless or pale yellow, oily, explosive liquid most commonly produced by nitrating glycerol with white fuming nitric acid under conditions appropriate to the formation of the nitric acid ester. Chemically, the substance is a nitrate ester rather than a nitro compound, but the traditional name is retained. Discovered in 1846 by Ascanio Sobrero, nitroglycerin has been used as an active ingredient in the manufacture of explosives, namely dynamite, and as such it is employed in the construction, demolition, and mining industries. It is combined with nitrocellulose to form double-based smokeless powder, used as a propellant in artillery and firearms since the 1880s.
As is the case for many other explosives, nitroglycerin becomes more and more prone to exploding (i.e., spontaneous decomposition) as the temperature is increased. Upon exposure to heat above 218 °C at sea-level atmospheric pressure, nitroglycerin becomes extremely unstable and tends to explode. When placed in vacuum, it has an autoignition temperature of 270 °C instead. With a melting point of 12.8 °C, the chemical is almost always encountered as a thick and viscous fluid, changing to a crystalline solid when frozen. Although the pure compound itself is colorless, in practice the presence of nitric oxide impurities left over during production tends to give it a slight yellowish tint.
Due to its high boiling point and consequently low vapor pressure (0.00026 mmHg at 20 °C), pure nitroglycerin has practically no odor at room temperature, with a sweet and burning taste when ingested. Unintentional detonation may ensue when dropped, shaken, lit on fire, rapidly heated, exposed to sunlight and ozone, subjected to sparks and electrical discharges, or roughly handled. Its sensitivity to exploding is responsible for numerous devastating industrial accidents throughout its history. The chemical's characteristic reactivity may be reduced through the addition of desensitizing agents, which makes it less likely to explode. Clay (diatomaceous earth) is an example of such an agent, forming dynamite, a much more easily handled composition. The addition of other desensitizing agents gives birth to the various formulations of dynamite.
Nitroglycerin as a medication has been used since 1878 as a potent vasodilator (causing dilation of the vascular system) to treat heart conditions, such as angina pectoris and chronic heart failure. Though it was previously known that these beneficial effects are due to nitroglycerin being converted to nitric oxide, a potent vasodilator, the enzyme for this conversion was only discovered to be mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2) in 2002. Nitroglycerin is available in sublingual tablets, sprays, ointments, and patches.

It appears as a colorless to pale yellow oily liquid with a density of 1.6 g/cmÂ³ that decomposes explosively at around 218 Â°C, generating gases expanding to over 1,200 times its original volume under extreme pressure and temperature. First synthesized in 1847 by Italian chemist Ascanio Sobrero through nitration of glycerol with a mixture of nitric and sulfuric acids, nitroglycerin was initially recognized for its violent explosive power upon percussion or shock, prompting Sobrero's reluctance to promote its industrial use due to safety risks. Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel later addressed its instability by absorbing it into kieselguhr to create dynamite in 1867, enabling safer handling and transforming applications in mining, construction, and demolition by providing a more controllable high explosive superior to black powder. Despite these advances, nitroglycerin's inherent volatility caused numerous fatal accidents, including explosions at Nobel's own facilities, underscoring the challenges of its causal detonation mechanism driven by rapid decomposition into nitrogen, carbon dioxide, water vapor, and oxygen. In pharmacology, nitroglycerin serves as a potent vasodilator; small, controlled doses of 0.3â0.6 mg in sublingual tablets relieve angina pectoris by relaxing vascular smooth muscle via nitric oxide release. Therapeutic use for angina was pioneered in 1879 by William Murrell, following Thomas Lauder Brunton's 1867 work with amyl nitrite, though its dual role as both destroyer and healer highlights the empirical balance between dose-dependent toxicity and efficacy. Its production remains tightly regulated due to explosive hazards, with modern formulations often incorporating stabilizers, yet pure nitroglycerin exemplifies the intersection of chemical reactivity and practical utility.
